lesson.title: How Much Bigger? Measuring Power Gain in Amplifiers
lesson.summary: Power gain compares the power delivered to a load against the power supplied at the input, and because that ratio can span many orders of magnitude, it is almost always expressed in decibels.
lesson.body:
Every amplifier is, at its core, a device that controls a large flow of power using a small controlling signal. A microphone might deliver only a few microwatts of electrical power, yet the same signal, after amplification, can drive a loudspeaker with several watts. The question "how much bigger did the power get" is answered by power gain.

Power gain is defined simply as the ratio of output power to input power: Ap = Pout / Pin. Because it is a ratio of the same units, it is dimensionless, and because power ratios in real systems can range from less than one (a lossy cable) to many millions (a multi-stage amplifier chain), engineers almost never report the raw ratio. Instead, they convert it to decibels using Ap(dB) = 10 log10(Pout / Pin), the factor of ten reflecting that decibels were originally defined around power ratios.

Consider a small amplifier stage that receives 2 milliwatts at its input and delivers 200 milliwatts to its load. The power gain ratio is Pout / Pin = 200 mW / 2 mW = 100. In decibels, that is 10 log10(100) = 10 times 2 = 20 dB. A clean, round number like this is common in textbook examples precisely because powers of ten convert so simply: every factor of 10 in power adds exactly 10 dB.

It is worth pausing on where that extra 198 milliwatts of output power actually comes from, since energy cannot be created from nothing. It is drawn from the amplifier's DC power supply, not manufactured from the input signal itself. The input signal does not supply the power delivered to the load, it merely controls how much of the supply's power is released to the load at each instant. This is the essential difference between an amplifier and, say, a transformer: an amplifier is an active, controlled valve for power, not a passive redistribution of the power that is already present.

Power gain alone does not tell the whole story of what an amplifier does to a signal, since a given amount of power gain can be produced by many different combinations of voltage and current gain. The next chapter breaks power gain apart into its two components, voltage gain and current gain, and shows precisely how they combine to reconstruct the same power gain figure from more detailed measurements.
